conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that there is no convincing evidence that ginkgo extract relieves tinnitus symptoms and notes that existing trials do not support its use, aligning with guidelines recommending against it.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: no convincing evidence shows that ginkgo extract reliably relieves tinnitus symptoms.** The best synthesis of randomized, placebo-controlled evidence (the Cochrane review) found too little and too uncertain evidence to establish a meaningful benefit. In other words, existing trials do not support expecting ginkgo to reduce tinnitus severity versus placebo reliably.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus

Why this is the appropriate conclusion:

- Individual randomized trials have produced mixed results, but inconsistent findings—especially across different extracts, doses, and study designs—do not establish efficacy. A systematic review specifically assessed placebo-controlled trials for that reason.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/

- An earlier Cochrane review/meta-analysis concluded that the limited evidence did **not** demonstrate ginkgo’s effectiveness when tinnitus was the main complaint.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23543524/

- Clinical guidance aligns with this evidence assessment: the AAO-HNS tinnitus guideline says clinicians should **not recommend ginkgo biloba or other dietary supplements** for persistent, bothersome tinnitus.  
https://www.entnet.org/quality-practice/quality-products/clinical-practice-guidelines/tinnitus/

This does not prove ginkgo can never help any individual, but it means a benefit has not been demonstrated well enough to recommend it as a tinnitus treatment.
